subject: physics_2
question_text: Find intensity of magnetic induction B due to a long current carrying conductor.

verification.note: The 1+1+1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. For this paper the two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are both STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers. Physics hand-checked: on a circle of radius r round a long straight wire, B is constant in magnitude and along dl, so ∮B·dl = B(2πr) = μ₀i and B = μ₀i/2πr, falling off as 1/r — matches the book. The book's 'inversly' spelling is corrected here.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.
insider_note: The symmetry sentence carries a mark on its own: say that B has the same magnitude everywhere on the circle and is along the tangent, before you take B out of the integral.

steps.label: The wire and a circle round it
steps.margin_note: A long straight wire carrying current i, a circle of radius r through the point P with the wire at its centre, and B along the tangent at P.
steps.why: The circle is chosen, not given: it is the one path on which B has the same size everywhere, which is what lets B come out of the integral.
common_mistakes: Drawing B along the radius. B is along the tangent to the circle.
Measuring r along the wire. It is the perpendicular distance from the wire to P.

recall.must_convey: That a long straight wire is drawn with a circle of radius r round it through P, and B tangential at P.
accept: draw the wire and a circle of radius r
reject: B equals mu nought i by two pi r

steps.memory_tip: Wire through the middle, circle round it, B running along the circle.

steps.label: The circle and the symmetry
steps.mark_note: Same B all round, along the tangent
lines: Let a long straight conductor carry a current
i, and let P be a point at a perpendicular
distance r from it.
Draw a circle of radius r through P with the
conductor as its centre.
The field at any point of this circle is
along the tangent drawn at that point, which
is the direction of dl.
By symmetry every point of the circle is the
same distance from the wire, so the magnitude
of B is the same at all points of the circle.
steps.margin_note: First mark. Two facts: B is along the tangent, and B has the same magnitude all the way round.
steps.why: Every point of the circle looks the same to the wire, so the field can only differ in direction, not in size — that is what symmetry gives here.
common_mistakes: Saying B points away from the wire. The field lines are closed circles round the wire.
Taking r along the wire instead of at right angles to it.

recall.must_convey: That a circle of radius r is drawn round the wire, B is tangential and B has the same magnitude at all its points.
accept: circle of radius r with the wire at its centre
same magnitude at all points by symmetry
reject: B into two pi r equals mu nought i

steps.memory_tip: Every point of the circle is the same distance out, so every point has the same B.

steps.label: The line integral
lines: B and dl point the same way at every point,
so the angle between them is 0°.

lines.text: ∮ B · dl = ∮ B dl cos 0° = B ∮ dl

lines: The total length of the circle is 2πr, so
steps.margin_note: Second mark. cos 0° = 1, B comes out of the integral, and ∮dl is the circumference.
steps.why: Two separate facts are used here: the same direction removes the cosine, and the same magnitude lets B be taken outside the integral.
common_mistakes: Writing cos 90°, which would make the whole integral zero.
Writing ∮dl = πr² — that is the area, not the length of the path.

recall.must_convey: That ∮B·dl becomes B times 2πr because cos 0° = 1 and B is constant.
accept: B comes out of the integral

steps.memory_tip: Same direction kills the cosine, same size frees the B.

steps.label: Ampere's law applied
lines: By Ampere's law the same line integral equals
μ₀ times the current enclosed by the path.
Here the circle encloses the current i, so
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Set the two expressions for the same integral equal to each other.
steps.why: One integral has now been written in two ways — once from the geometry and once from Ampere's law — and equating them is what produces the answer.
common_mistakes: Putting μ₀ on the left with B. It multiplies the current.
Using the total current in the circuit instead of the current through the circle.

recall.must_convey: That Ampere's law gives the same integral as μ₀i, so B(2πr) = μ₀i.
accept: by ampere's law equals mu nought i
B into two pi r equals mu nought i
reject: B equals mu nought i by two pi r

steps.memory_tip: The same integral, two ways: geometry on one side, Ampere on the other.

steps.label: The result
lines: So B is directly proportional to the current
and inversely proportional to the
perpendicular distance from the wire.
The direction is given by the right hand
rule: hold the wire in the right hand with
the thumb along the current, and the curled
fingers give the direction of B.
steps.margin_note: Last mark. The boxed result, the 1/r dependence and one line on direction.
steps.why: The field of a single wire falls off as 1/r, not as 1/r², because the source is a whole line of current rather than a single point.
common_mistakes: Writing 1/r² for a straight wire. The inverse square belongs to a current element, not to the whole wire.
Leaving out the direction rule when the question asks for the induction B.

recall.must_convey: That B = μ₀i/2πr, falling off as 1/r, with the direction from the right hand rule.
accept: B equals mu nought i by two pi r
B is inversely proportional to r
right hand rule gives the direction
reject: B into two pi r equals mu nought i
heard_as: mu nought i by two pi r

steps.memory_tip: Divide by the circumference: μ₀i shared out over 2πr.
